text:
olivia: Heads-up from NimbusOps: customers reporting odd rounding on marketplace invoices after we switched to hourly billing. Looks like partial-minute activity at hour boundaries isn't being prorated correctly. Need a clear playbook for prorate rules, rounding, and reconciliation.

ben: Quick background: previously partner sent per-minute counts and we used minute->hour naive sum. After migrating to hour-fraction units (hours with 8 decimals) a few edge cases appear: (A) devices that are active for only part of a minute (firmware reports fractional pulses), (B) minutes that straddle hour boundary due to tz vs UTC normalization, (C) repeated retransmit of the same minute from aggregator causing overcount.

samir: Sample edge case: device active from 12:59:30 -> 13:00:20 (50s total). Partner's minute-agg: minute 12:59 -> 30s pulse, minute 13:00 -> 20s pulse. Adapter currently converts each minute to 0.01666667 hours (1min), losing fractional intra-minute duration. Correct approach: compute precise fractional hours from per-second pulses or use proportional allocation when only minute totals provided.

katie: Practical options:
- If partner provides per-second pulses: reconstruct exact seconds active and compute hours precisely.
- If only minute buckets: prorate boundary minutes by estimating fraction: e.g., minute_count * (overlap_seconds / 60). Requires partner to indicate exact start/end within minute or provide per-second samples for boundary windows.

olivia: We need to pick defaults for marketplace ingestion when partner cannot provide fine-grained timestamps. Proposal: assume uniform distribution within minute except when device reports session start/end markers. For minute buckets that overlap hour boundary, split proportionally (e.g., minute 12:59 => 30s attributed to hour12 and 30s to hour13 if overlap). Document assumption clearly for partners and in legal.

ben: Rounding rules: persist qty as decimal string with 8 decimals of hours. For aggregation to invoiceable hours, sum up fractions using decimal arithmetic (avoid float). Round final invoice line to 6 decimals for readability but keep full precision in ledger for auditing.

samir: Security/replay safeguards: require usage_key computed as sha256(partner_id + device_id + start_iso + end_iso + seq_id) where available. Ingest upsert by usage_key. Signature header X-Partner-Sig required. Example ingestion payload (compact):
```json
{"usage_batch": [
  {"usage_key":"sha256(...)","sku":"nimbus-edge-hour","start":"2026-04-01T12:59:30Z","end":"2026-04-01T13:00:20Z","qty":"0.01388889","unit":"hours"}
]}
```
Note qty here equals 50s -> 50/3600 = 0.0138888889 -> rounded to 8 decimals.

katie: Reconciliation plan:
- Daily reconcile job at 00:30 UTC comparing partner-provided minute/second aggregates vs our invoiceable hours for the prior day.
- Metrics: absolute delta (hours), percent delta, top N customers by delta.
- Thresholds: auto-adjust if delta <= 0.5% and delta_hours < 5 hours; create billing-review card if 0.5% < delta <= 2% OR delta_hours between 5-50h; escalate to ops+finance+legal if delta > 2% OR delta_hours > 50h. These numbers are starters; finance/legal to review.

ben: Backfill approach when partner provides higher-resolution archives:
1) Dry-run: run transform on partner archive into our canonical usage_batch and surface diffs for pilot customers.
2) If diffs look correct, produce adjustment events (negative/positive) to correct ledgers and emit audit CSV.
3) Notify customers flagged in scope with transparent adjustment breakdown.
4) Apply adjustments in next billing cycle, or sooner if finance/legal approves immediate credits.

olivia: Edge case: regulated customers (EU public sector) require explicit consent for retroactive credits. We must flag accounts with "no-auto-adjust" in tenant metadata and route any corrections to manual review. Add to runbook.

samir: Example boundary handling pseudo-algo when only minute buckets present:
- For each minute bucket overlapping two hours, estimate overlap by looking at session start/end markers if provided; otherwise assume uniform distribution and split minute proportionally.
- Convert fractional minutes to hours with 8-decimal rounding per minute, then sum to hour.
- Emit usage_key for each minute-fragment so later dedupe works at fragment granularity.

katie: Implementation owners & ETA:
- samir: proto change to accept start/end timestamps and minute-fragment mode in adapter + signer verification (ETA 48h)
- ben: ledger rounding library + audit CSV output + backfill runner (ETA 72h)
- olivia: partner comms + legal loop + create "no-auto-adjust" account flag (ETA 48h)
- katie: dashboard panels + reconcile job + pager rule (ETA 72h)

billing-bot: Created ticket PARTNER-PRORATE-1765 and scheduled daily-reconcile job at 00:30 UTC.

ben: Example cURL ingest for partner (with signature header):
```bash
curl -X POST https://ingest.redwood.ai/partner/usage \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "X-Partner-Sig: <base64sig>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @usage_batch.json
```
Server responses: 202 Accepted (batch queued), 400 PT-400-MISSINGTIMESTAMPS (if no start/end and minute_bucket ambiguous), 409 PT-409-DUPLICATE (if usage_key exists).

samir: Tests to add: fractional-second sessions, minute-only buckets with implied uniform split, per-second pulse input path, heavy boundary spikes (topology where thousands of devices flip at hh:00), and tenant metadata flag respecting. Include property-based tests for summation closure (sum of fragments == full session within epsilon).

olivia: I'll schedule partner sync tomorrow 8am PT to align on start/end fields and the "no-auto-adjust" tenant metadata. Also will send draft partner-facing FAQ explaining why prorating matters and timeline for fixes/adjustments.

katie: I'll mock dashboard and run reconcile dry-run with a small dataset; will post screenshots to the Jira ticket.

ben: Anything else? If not I'll start the ledger lib PR and document the decimal rules in the API spec.

olivia: Great. Please keep comms transparent. This should be a low-friction customer experience. Thanks all.
